summary: Describes a framework for making Integrated Services, which reserve resources for individual flows, work across networks that use Differentiated Services, which treat traffic by class. It explains how reservations made at the edges can be honored across a Diffserv region. It is informational guidance, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how per-flow resource requests can cross a Diffserv network that handles packets in classes. RSVP carries requests end to end, while edge or border routers decide whether the Diffserv region has enough resources.

questions: how do intserv and diffserv work together
what is admission control in qos
what is a service level specification
how do rsvp reservations cross diffserv networks
subtitle: A framework for carrying per-flow RSVP reservations across networks that handle traffic by class.

tldr.problem: Integrated Services can reserve resources per flow, but per-flow state raises scalability concerns. Diffserv scales by class, but does not itself signal whether an individual request can be admitted.
tldr.mechanism: The framework treats each Diffserv region as a virtual link for Intserv. RSVP messages cross it, edge or border routers perform admission control, and Intserv services map to Diffserv behaviors.
tldr.outcome: The Informational memo describes statically provisioned, RSVP-aware and oracle-based approaches, along with requirements and multicast difficulties. It is a framework, not a protocol specification.

facts.label: Resource-management approaches
facts.value: Static provisioning, RSVP or other dynamic means

today: RFC 2998 is an Informational framework memo from November 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Intserv, RSVP and Diffserv
sections.content:
Integrated Services (Intserv) defines controlled-load and guaranteed services and assumes a setup mechanism for conveying resource needs. RSVP is a signaling protocol that carries such requests. Intserv-capable routers can admit or reject each flow and classify packets using addresses and port numbers.

Differentiated Services (Diffserv) classifies packets into a small number of groups using the DSCP in the IP header. Routers apply a per-hop behavior to each group. This aggregate approach avoids per-flow state and is designed to scale across large networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Intserv asks for resources for individual flows and can return an admission decision. Diffserv handles packets in a small number of classes, which reduces per-flow work in the network.

sections.title: Why Combine the Architectures
sections.content:
A Diffserv region can be provisioned to accept a fixed amount of traffic for a service class, but static policing does not identify which flow exceeded the limit. The RFC gives an example with 10 telephony sessions requesting 10 Kbps each and an EF limit of 50 Kbps: half the offered traffic may be discarded without regard to which session sent it.

With explicit RSVP signaling, the network can reject requests that exceed available capacity, preserving admitted flows and allowing applications or hosts to adjust. RSVP can also help apply per-user or per-application policy, identify traffic for marking and condition each flow before it enters the Diffserv region.
sections.plainLanguage: Static limits can discard traffic without identifying which individual flow should be rejected. RSVP lets the network accept or reject each reservation request before traffic enters the Diffserv region.

sections.title: The Reference Network and Service Mapping
sections.content:
The reference network places a Diffserv region between Intserv-capable networks. Edge routers sit next to the region; border routers sit inside it. RSVP messages must pass across the region, but routers there may either ignore them or participate in signaling.

Service mapping converts an Intserv service type and flowspec into a Diffserv per-hop behavior, policing, admission control and any needed Intserv parameter updates. In an RSVP-unaware region, edge routers can act as admission control agents using resource information and customer policy. In an RSVP-aware region, border routers can make decisions using resources on the specific path.
sections.plainLanguage: A Diffserv region is treated as a virtual link between Intserv-capable nodes. Its edge or border routers map a reservation to a service class and decide whether to admit it.

sections.title: Reservations in a Statically Provisioned Region
sections.content:
In the first example, routers inside the Diffserv region do not understand RSVP. A customer and the region owner agree on a service level specification (SLS) that sets capacity for each service level. The customer edge router tracks the capacity available at each level.

The sender sends RSVP PATH toward the receiver. The receiver returns RESV. The RESV passes through the Diffserv region to the sending edge router, which checks the request against the remaining SLS capacity and customer policy. If admitted, the router updates its capacity table and forwards RESV toward the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender's request travels to the receiver, and the receiver's reservation travels back. The sending edge router checks the agreed capacity and policy before accepting the flow.

sections.title: Dynamic Management, Oracles and Multicast
sections.content:
An RSVP-aware Diffserv region can use aggregated RSVP between its edges, per-flow RSVP within the region, or an oracle such as a bandwidth broker. These choices trade signaling work against how precisely the network can track available resources. A region can also use an oracle reached through custom protocols.

The framework requires a Diffserv region to provide standard Intserv services between border routers, give customers admission-control information and carry RSVP messages to the egress. It must isolate Intserv, non-Intserv and best-effort traffic. Multicast is harder when branches need different service, because a core router using aggregate classification may not know which packets to demote.
sections.plainLanguage: A region can manage reservations with fixed capacity, RSVP signaling or an information service called an oracle. Multicast creates extra challenges when different receiver branches need different service.
